newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: LME aluminium seen heading higher on squeeze-trade.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium seen heading higher on squeeze-trade.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium prices are likely to head higher later on Tuesday on the back of a speculative squeeze, dealers said.
"We're heading for higher prices. I believe it's not the end yet," an aluminium dealer in Singapore said.
LME aluminium rose on Monday to a 22-month high at US$1,747 a tonne before settling $5 up on the day at $1,744. One metal house in Singapore quoted aluminium at 0236 GMT at $1,746/50.
"The funds are artificially squeezing out the market. It's like a balloon. You will one day have a big bang because the prices are not fundamentally justified," a trader said.

Rudolf Wolff said in its daily review that while the market was heavily overbought, the technical indicators "suggest further challenges of resistance between $1,745/50 a tonne". "Should this level be breached, buy stops are expected to be found, which could seen aluminium rally to tackle the next resistance levels between $1,765 and $1,770," it said.
Dealers said the steady fall of LME aluminium inventories were not matched by consumption, leading them to believe that speculative funds were involved in a squeeze in the market.

One trader said aluminium prices will rise because he heard several big metal trading houses had already "bought call options at $1,800 to $1,900 (a tonne) so they apparently believe that the market will head higher".
Another dealer said some people in the market may wait for options declaration on Wednesday to get a clue on aluminium's next move.
"For the moment, aluminium looks a little higher," he said.
Zinc prices were also likely to firm because of belief by the trade that some of the short positions belonging to the Chinese were still intact.
"The squeeze is still on," one dealer said. "There's still some tightness in September and the Chinese are definitely shipping stuff to the LME warehouse," in Singapore.
Some 5,000-10,000 tonnes of zinc remain off-warrant in warehouses in Singapore. The volume of zinc in the LME warehouse here reached 47,675 tonnes on Monday, down 175 tonnes from last Friday's level.
Copper prices, on the other hand, were seen range-bound on the LME with a downside bias, dealers said.
"It looks pretty weak. Some of my buyers who buy copper and zinc are not talking about copper at all," a dealer said.
Another trader added: "It looks pretty much range-bound. It's hovering on either side of $2,300."

Brokers Brandeis said in its daily review copper had a disappointing close on Monday and "a test of $2,250 seems likely in the near term. The next $2,225/30 area would then form the next layer of support, followed by $2,200."
The Asian base metal business was quiet, with one dealer saying the only recent business he'd seen was for several hundred tonnes of lead.
"The market is looking for a rest," a dealer said, adding the seasonal summer holiday period should keep things quiet.
